How this book matches your exam. IB Biology (guide first assessed in 2025) is organised into four themes: A Unity and diversity, B Form and function, C Interaction and interdependence, D Continuity and change. It is assessed as follows:

  • SL: Paper 1 (1h30, 55 marks: Paper 1A multiple choice and Paper 1B data-based questions), 36%; Paper 2 (1h30, 50 marks), 44%;
  • HL: Paper 1 (2h, 75 marks), 36%; Paper 2 (2h30, 80 marks), 44%;
  • both levels: the scientific investigation (internal assessment), 20%.

This book covers A1.1 Water, A1.2 Nucleic acids, B1.1 Carbohydrates and lipids, and B1.2 Proteins, with the HL extensions marked. The mark allocations are our own guides, written in the style of IB markschemes.

Unit 1 of 10: Water: Hydrogen Bonding and Cohesion

Key ideas

  • Polarity: water is a polar molecule. Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so oxygen carries a partial negative charge (δ−) and the hydrogens carry partial positive charges (δ+).
  • Hydrogen bonds: weak attractions between the δ+ hydrogen of one water molecule and the δ− oxygen of another.
  • Cohesion: water molecules stick to each other through hydrogen bonds. This allows:
  • transpiration pull in xylem, where columns of water are pulled up under tension;
  • surface tension, which supports small organisms such as pond skaters.
  • Adhesion: water sticks to other polar surfaces. This gives capillary action in narrow tubes and in soil, and helps water move through cell walls.
  • Life began in water: water was the medium in which the first cells arose.

Worked examples

Example 1: explaining transpiration pull: water evaporates from leaf cells. Cohesion between water molecules transmits the pull down the continuous water column in the xylem, so water is drawn up from the roots.

Example 2: explaining why a pond skater does not sink: hydrogen bonds at the water surface create surface tension that supports its weight.

Example 3: explaining capillary action: adhesion to the walls of a narrow tube (or to soil particles) draws water upwards against gravity.

10-mark exam-style question

(a) Draw a labelled diagram showing hydrogen bonding between two water molecules. [3]

(b) Distinguish between cohesion and adhesion, with one biological example of each. [4]

(c) Explain why the polarity of water is essential for xylem transport. [3]

Answers:

  • (a) Two V-shaped molecules, with δ− on O and δ+ on each H. A dashed line joins the H of one molecule to the O of the other, labelled "hydrogen bond" (A3).
  • (b) Cohesion is attraction between water molecules (for example, transpiration pull in xylem) (A2). Adhesion is attraction between water and other polar substances (for example, capillary action in soil or cell walls) (A2).
  • (c) Polarity allows hydrogen bonds between water molecules. These give cohesion, so the water column in the xylem can be pulled up under tension without breaking (R3).

Common mistakes

  1. Drawing the hydrogen bond as a covalent bond within one molecule.
  2. Mixing up cohesion and adhesion.
  3. Leaving out partial charges in diagrams.
  4. Saying hydrogen bonds are strong (they are individually weak, but there are many).
  5. Giving no biological example.

Quick recall

  1. Why is water polar?
  2. What is a hydrogen bond?
  3. What does cohesion allow in plants?
  4. What causes capillary action?
  5. What supports a pond skater?

Answers: 1) Oxygen is more electronegative, giving partial charges. 2) A weak attraction between a δ+ H and a δ− O on different molecules. 3) Transpiration pull in xylem. 4) Adhesion. 5) Surface tension.
